# Likert attitudes as controls in the punishment regressions

**Exploration, not a manuscript artefact.** Generated by
`explorations/likert_controls_regressions.py`. Question: what happens to the
punishment regressions when Player B's three post-experiment Likert items
(`responsibility`, `trust`, `perception`) enter individually and jointly?

**Sample.** Punishment condition (`treat == 0`), attention-check passers
(`pass_att2 == 1`), the preregistered sample of the main punishment table
(Column 2 of `tables/reg_punishment.tex`): n = 67 Player Bs. Standard
errors clustered at the Player B level. Cells report coefficient (SE) [p].
No significance stars, per AEA convention.

**Caveat on timing.** The Likert items were elicited *after* the punishment
decisions. They are post-treatment measurements of attitudes, not exogenous
controls, so these regressions describe associations and cannot support a
causal reading.

estimation sample to isolate that channel.

## Reading

1. **The dominant effect of including the Likert items is sample loss, not
   coefficient movement.** The three items were only collected in the main
   wave; all 23 pilot-wave Player Bs in the analysis sample are missing all
   three (structural missingness, verified against the `pilot` flag). Any
   specification with a Likert item therefore drops from 67 to 44 subjects
   and cannot use the pooled pilot+main sample.

2. **The design coefficients do not react to the Likert controls at all.**
   In Panel A, columns (2)-(5) are identical to column (6), the baseline
   refit on the same 44-subject sample, to the third decimal (Delegated
   0.045, Delegated x Bad -0.062). The apparent movement relative to
   column (1) (Delegated 0.001 -> 0.045, interaction -0.078 -> -0.062) is
   entirely the wave restriction. This is as expected: the items are
   between-subject constants, orthogonal by construction to the
   within-subject design dummies.

3. **None of the items predicts punishment levels individually**
   (p = 0.83, 0.34, 0.32). Jointly, trust (-0.178, p = 0.119) and
   perception (+0.191, p = 0.065) both inflate relative to their individual
   coefficients, a mutual-suppression pattern driven by their correlation
   (r = 0.43). The marginal perception coefficient should not be
   over-read: joint spec only, N = 44, post-treatment measurement.
   The responsibility item is a precise zero throughout Panel A.

4. **No moderation.** In Panel B, no Likert item predicts the size of the
   within-subject delegation effect (all p >= 0.14). In particular, the
   responsibility item ("how responsible should Player A feel?") does not
   predict whether a subject punishes self-made decisions more than
   delegated ones (0.044, p = 0.58 in the joint spec). This matches the
   correlational null in `15_player_b_attitudes.py`.

5. **Other movements in Panel B are also composition, not controls.** The
   socio-economic-status coefficient roughly doubles and becomes
   significant (~0.08, p ~ 0.01-0.03) once the sample restricts to the
   main wave, but it does so already in the column-(6) baseline. Same for
   the adjusted R2 jump (0.04 -> 0.18): column (6) shows 0.18 without any
   Likert regressor.

**Bottom line.** The punishment results are robust to including the
attitude items; the items themselves carry essentially no explanatory
power for the delegation-related coefficients. Adding them to the main
table would buy nothing and cost the pilot wave. If used at all, they fit
best as a brief appendix/footnote robustness remark, with the moderation
null (point 4) the most quotable piece.
